cards.title: California is chasing wealth that has feet

depth.text: the article says California should tax **land** instead of chasing **billionaires** who can leave

The Center for Land Economics estimates California’s land is worth **$8.14 trillion** and argues a **0.25 percent land value tax** could raise the same $20 billion a year as the proposed wealth tax. It says land can’t leave the state, while billionaires can, and blames **Proposition 13** for weakening the property-tax base.

cards.camps: Two camps: land-tax supporters see a stable tax that can’t move; skeptics question land valuation and homeowner costs, or say the wealth-tax proposal shouldn’t be rejected when a land-tax measure isn’t on this ballot.

comments.text: Land, as apposed to the property on it, is raw nature. If we view raw nature as a common inheritance of mankind, then paying a tax on land is how the exclusionary use of it, balances with the common interest in it. Economist Henry George in the 1800's, pointed out that taxing land, but not the property on it, incentivizes efficient use of land, because holding land for its passive (parasitic)…

> The land value tax can’t be dodged by leaving nor can it be passed on to renters. In what sense can't it be passed to renters? Esp if all landlords in the market were faced with a new land tax that they had not previously planned for, why would it not be passed on?

Wealth taxes are a symptom of a broken tax system. If you let someone get to hundreds of billions in net worth and then realize they haven’t been appropriately paying back into the system, it’s already too late. Like the article says they can simply say “no” in a variety of ways, from fighting in court to simply leaving.

Property tax increases are hamstrung by Prop 13 and until that’s repealed, will continue to be. And while the wealthy always threaten to leave when faced with higher taxes, the fact is that they never seem to actually do so. cards.title: Creatine uptake enhances antitumor immunity

depth.text: a study links **creatine uptake** to **antitumor immunity**, though commenters say the evidence cuts both ways

One commenter says the mice got **10mg per day**, around 3g per day for a 70kg human. Another cites reports that **cancer cells can use creatine as fuel** and that creatine promoted mouse cancer models; they say effects may depend on cancer type, with **no human data either way**.
data: around 3g per day for a 70kg human

cards.camps: Two camps: some find the immune result interesting; others point to reports that creatine may help tumors too and say effects could vary by cancer type.

cards.title: Disney+ and Hulu raise prices by up to 13 percent after doubling profits

depth.text: Disney+ and Hulu are **raising subscription prices** again, even as their **combined operating income** jumped

Standalone **ad-free plans** rise 13 percent, from $19 per month to **$21.50/month**; ad-supported plans go from $12 to $12.50. The Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Select bundle without ads goes from $29 to $33, while combined operating income rose **116 percent** year over year to $712 million.
data: Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Select bundle without ads
116 percent year over year to $712 million

cards.camps: Two camps: some say price hikes make streaming not worth it and push people toward piracy; others say Disney+ and Hulu are still good value, especially for families or compared with cable.

cards.title: Virtio-nvgpu: Near-native Nvidia GPU access inside a KVM guest

depth.text: someone built an **experimental way** for virtual machines to **share an NVIDIA GPU** at near-native speed

It forwards NVIDIA driver requests at the **driver level**, so guests use NVIDIA’s unmodified user-mode drivers instead of translating graphics calls. On the tested RTX 3060, frames over about 2 ms came within **2%** of bare metal. But there’s no IOMMU boundary between guest GPU work and the host, so this is **not hardware isolation**.

comments.text: There are roughly 3 ways to give a KVM guest a GPU. 1) VFIO passthrough: host binds entire GPU to guest as PCI device, which only allows one VM to use the GPU, thus you sacrifice your host display too (unless you fallback to integrated graphics on cpu etc). Strongest isolation because host kernel module driver not involved. 2) virtio-gpu: guest sees paravirtual GPU and loads virgl/venus mesa…
Amazing project! But man, that README is just a textbook example of LLM word salad. It's wild how these tools are so incredibly capable at many things, but their writing sticks out like a sore thumb

I'm a guy with vague knowledge on KVM - having only tinkered with it and briefly had a GPU pass-through setup 2 years ago. I suggest putting the 'multiple guests at near-native speed' use-case in the opening paragraphs of the README.
Hrm, something of a lack of discussion about what level of access the card has to the host in the absence of IOMMU-restricted passthrough.

How is this different than gVisor's nvproxy? https://gvisor.dev/docs/user_guide/gpu/#compatibility Edit: nvproxy is mentioned as the "direct inspiration" in the readme without mention of how this is different or why it doesn't use nvproxy as a backend.

cards.title: Radicle: Disclosure of Vulnerability in the Network Protocol

depth.text: someone found **two security flaws** in Radicle that expose **private repos** and let attackers **fake peers**

Network traffic is sent in **plain text**, and a broken handshake can let someone who knows an allow-listed Node ID **fake that identity** and fetch a private repository. The team says to **stop using private repositories** over the network until a fix is released.

comments.text: > What is the issue? > Network traffic between nodes is not encrypted and not authenticated. Oh. After all of the work they put into using cryptographic identities and decentralization tricks, how did they forget to do anything about the network traffic? Was this a case of thinking they'd handle it later, but then it fell off the TODO list?

> This was reported to us by Konstantinos Maninakis on 2026-06-24. announcement 3 months later is not super great, considering that the current advice is "Stop using private repositories (over the network) until the security update is released."

The fact that this was reported three months ago and the "workaround" is to stop using private repos and assume they are all pwnd is quite something. How do you not notice that cross-node traffic is not encrypted when building something like this?

Radicle has been one of those projects that had seemed interesting, but something always bothered me about it. (I think it was very highly tied to the cryptocurrency movement for a while? And the Cyphernet GitHub org seems to have rebranded from a DAO?) This, unfortunately, kinda seals the deal on never using this thing, at least not for anything I intend to keep private. This isn't about…
This whole project reads like amateur hour. Still using curl pipe to shell install and everything. Plus this lax security disclosure with just an outstandingly foolish security flaw. Gross.

glossary.land value tax: A property tax charged only on the land itself, not on the buildings sitting on it.
glossary.wealth flight: When wealthy people move themselves or their money away so a tax can’t reach it.
glossary.assessed value: The value officials assign to a property when working out its property tax.
glossary.tax base: The pool of money or property a government can collect a tax from.
glossary.HTML: HyperText Markup Language: code that tells a browser what content a web page has.
glossary.serverless agent: An AI-powered program that a web service runs when needed, without you managing the computer it runs on.
glossary.microVM: A small, separate computer environment for running a job; here, it gets thrown away when the job ends.
glossary.virtual clock: A clock controlled by a program so it can replay an animation at chosen moments.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.ffmpeg: A tool that can turn pictures and sound into a video file.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.sprite art: Pictures of game characters or objects that can move around separately on screen.
glossary.pixel art: Pictures built from visible colored squares, often with a blocky look.
glossary.easter egg: A hidden joke or surprise tucked into a game or website.
glossary.Konami code: A sequence of button presses used as a hidden shortcut or surprise in a game.
glossary.random walk: A route made by taking one random step after another.
glossary.creatine: A substance muscles use for quick energy, also taken as a supplement.
glossary.antitumor immunity: The body's immune defenses working against tumors.
glossary.in vitro: Done in a lab outside a living body, often using cells in a dish.
glossary.ATP: Adenosine triphosphate: a substance cells use to supply energy.
glossary.metastasis: Cancer spreading from where it started to other parts of the body.
glossary.vibe-coding: Making software with an AI's help by describing what you want and steering the results.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.fps: Frames per second: how many still images the screen shows each second; more usually makes motion look smoother.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.UX: User experience: how using a product feels and how easy it is to get things done.
glossary.4K: A screen picture with much more detail than standard HD.
glossary.HDR: High Dynamic Range: a way for a screen to show more detail in bright and dark areas.
glossary.operating income: Money a company makes from its main business after paying the costs of running it.
glossary.bundle: A group of services sold together for one price.
glossary.KVM: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: a Linux feature for running virtual machines.
glossary.virtio: A way for a virtual machine to exchange data with devices provided by its host.
glossary.ioctl: A request a program sends to a device driver to ask it to do something.
glossary.IOMMU: Input-Output Memory Management Unit: hardware that restricts which memory a device can access.
glossary.bare metal: Running directly on a physical machine rather than inside a virtual machine.
glossary.NVENC: A part of some NVIDIA GPUs that turns video frames into compressed video.
glossary.ABI: Application Binary Interface: the agreed rules software uses to communicate with other software.
glossary.plain text: Data sent without protection that would stop someone watching the connection from reading it.
glossary.handshake: The first exchange where two computers check who they are talking to.
glossary.allow-listed Node ID: A name for a computer that has been approved to fetch a private repository.
glossary.peer-to-peer: A setup where computers talk directly to each other instead of relying on one central server.
